title: Conditional Probability and the Restricted Sample Space
quickIdea: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B), defined only when P(B) > 0. Learning that B happened throws away every outcome outside B and rescales what is left so that it still sums to 1.
remember: The definition is a ratio of two probabilities of the same space: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It is a ratio of counts, |A and B| / |B|, only when the outcomes are equally likely.
The denominator is P(B), the probability of the condition. Putting the probability of the event you want there is the commonest error in the topic.
Conditioning shrinks the sample space to B. An outcome outside B is no longer possible, so it stops counting anywhere - not in the numerator and not in the denominator.

Two ways to compute the same thing: restrict first and count inside B, or take the ratio of the two unconditional probabilities. They must agree, and disagreement means one of them used the wrong space.
P(A|B) exists only when P(B) > 0. A zero-probability condition cannot revise anything, which is why the definition carries the caveat.
P(A|B) and P(B|A) share the same numerator P(A and B) and are still different numbers: one is a share of B, the other a share of A.
P(A|B) >= P(A and B) always, because dividing by P(B) <= 1 can only enlarge the number.

example.prompt: A fair die is rolled. B is the event that an even number appears and E is the event that 2 appears. Compare P(E) with P(E|B).
example.work: Unconditionally P(E) = 1/6, because 2 is one of six equally likely faces. Given B, the possible faces are 2, 4 and 6 only, so the space has three outcomes and 2 is one of them: P(E|B) = |{2}| / |{2,4,6}| = 1/3. By the formula, P(E and B) = 1/6 and P(B) = 1/2, so P(E|B) = (1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3.
example.answer: P(E) = 1/6 and P(E|B) = 1/3; the information doubled the probability.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2011 Q.3 is this card in one line: two fair coins, 'at least one of the outcomes is known to be a head', and the answer is 1/3 - not 1/2 (which forgets that HH is one of three survivors) and not 1/4 (which forgets the condition altogether).

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2011 Q.3: two fair coins are flipped and at least one outcome is known to be a head. What is the probability that both outcomes are heads?
variations.why: The four outcomes are equally likely; the condition removes TT and leaves HH, HT, TH. Exactly one of the three survivors is HH.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the sum is 8, what is the probability that the first die shows 3?
variations.why: The ordered outcomes with sum 8 are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2): five of them. Only (3,5) has first die 3, so the restricted space gives 1/5. This is the worked example on the Knowledge Gate GATE page.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: In the dice example above, why is 1/36 the wrong answer, and what does it actually compute?
variations.answer: 1/36 is P(first die 3 and sum 8), the unconditional probability of the single outcome (3,5). The question asks for a share of the five outcomes that already satisfy the condition, so the denominator must be 5, not 36.
variations.why: This is the whole content of the definition: the condition replaces the space.

trap.what: Dividing by the wrong space - using P(A) in the denominator, or the full space when the question has already restricted it.
trap.why: The condition is information about which outcomes are still possible. The definition normalises by exactly that information, so the denominator is the probability of the condition.
trap.counterexample: For the two coins of GATE CSE 2011 Q.3, P(both heads) / P(at least one head) = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3, but P(both heads)/P(both heads) = 1 and P(both heads)/1 = 1/4 are the two wrong denominators in their purest form.

check.question: Two fair dice are rolled and the sum is known to be 9. What is the probability that the first die shows 4?
check.explanation: The outcomes with sum 9 are (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3) - four of them, all equally likely. Exactly one has first die 4, so the probability is 1/4. Equivalently (1/36)/(4/36) = 1/4.
